summary: This unit helps you, as a Level 3 electrician, plan the move from working for someone else to running your own electrical contracting firm. You will assess yourself honestly, set SMART goals and a five-year plan, choose a niche, research the market and set the business up legally. You will also cost and price jobs, work out break-even and cash flow, prepare a business plan for a lender, win and keep work, and review and grow the business safely.

blocks.p: Many electricians in Jamaica want to run their own firm. Some do well; many struggle, not because their wiring is poor but because they price too low, run out of cash or never plan. This unit is about planning. A **personal entrepreneurial strategy** is your own written plan for getting from where you are now to owning and running a business: what you want, what you have, what you lack, and the steps, dates and money needed to close the gap.

It is a Level 3 unit, so you are expected to do the sums yourself (costs, charge-out rate, mark-up, margin, break-even and cash flow), to judge risks, and to explain your choices to a lender, a partner or a client.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like in practice
rows: Decide whether running a business suits you
Compare life as an employee and as an owner, and talk honestly with your family about the risk, the hours and the money.
Assess yourself
Carry out a skills audit and a personal SWOT analysis, and use them to decide what to build on and what to fix.
Set goals and milestones
Write SMART goals and a five-year plan with yearly milestones for your licence, experience, savings, equipment and first clients.
Choose a niche and research the market
Find out who needs what kind of electrical work in your area, who the competitors are, and what will make customers choose you.
Set the business up legally
Hold the licence the law requires for your work, choose a business structure, register the business and for tax, open a business bank account and buy the right insurance.
Cost and price work
Separate direct costs from overheads, work out a charge-out rate, build up a job price with contingency and profit, and tell mark-up from margin.
Plan the money
Prepare a start-up budget, choose sources of finance, work out break-even and build a cash flow forecast.
Prepare a business plan
Put the strategy and the figures into a plan that a lender or partner can judge.
Win and keep work
Market the business, write quotations and tenders, agree contracts and variations, and handle complaints.
Run, review and grow the business
Keep records, meet your duties as an employer, manage risk, compare results with the plan and decide when to grow.

blocks.p: The theory papers test your understanding and your sums: multiple-choice questions, short answers (terms such as gross profit, debtors, retention and working capital, and short calculations) and essays in which you plan, explain and give examples. In the practical tasks you write a personal SWOT, research your local market, choose a niche and present SMART goals and five-year milestones on a poster. Then, as a team, you prepare a start-up budget, a charge-out rate, a break-even figure, a six-month cash flow forecast and a priced quotation, and present them to a 'loan officer'.

blocks.note: Practise every calculation in this kit with a calculator until you can do it without the notes, and always show your working. In an exam, a loan meeting or a quotation, a figure without working cannot be checked.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: The figures in this kit are examples in Jamaican dollars (J$). Prices, wages, tax rates and fees change. When you plan for real, use current prices from suppliers and the current rates and rules from Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) and the other bodies named here, and check them with your instructor.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An **entrepreneur** is someone who spots an opportunity, takes a measured risk, and organises money, skills and people to turn it into a business. For an electrician, that usually means moving from wiring for an employer to winning, pricing, running and guaranteeing the work yourself.

head: Point
As an employee
As an owner
rows: Income
A regular wage, paid whether the firm is busy or not.
Irregular at first. You are paid only after customers pay and the bills are met.
Hours
Set hours; overtime is paid.
Long hours: quoting, buying, paperwork and chasing payment come on top of the wiring.
Risk
The employer carries the debts, the insurance and the bad jobs.
You carry them. A bad debt, an accident or a faulty job is your problem.
Decisions
Mostly made for you.
Yours: which jobs to take, what to charge, whom to hire.
Rewards
Fixed.
The profit is yours, the firm can grow, and you build something you can sell or pass on.

ul: **Initiative**: you look for work instead of waiting for it.
**Measured risk-taking**: you take risks you have worked out and can survive, not gambles.
**Persistence**: you keep going through slow months, lost tenders and late payers.
**Discipline with money**: you keep business and personal money apart and do not spend the deposit before the materials are bought.
**Honesty**: clients, suppliers, lenders and inspectors must be able to trust your word and your certificates.
**Customer focus and networking**: most work comes from people who know you, so you build and keep good relationships.
**Willingness to learn**: technology, codes and markets keep changing.

blocks.h: Routes into business for an electrician

head: Route
Points to know
rows: Weekend and evening jobs while employed
Builds clients, savings and confidence with little risk. Check your employment contract, and never take your employer's clients, materials or time.
Subcontracting to a larger contractor
Steady work and less marketing, but lower prices, and you depend on one firm paying you on time.
Partnership with another tradesperson
Shares cost, skills and work, for example two electricians with different strengths, or an electrician and a plumber. Needs a written agreement and trust.
Taking over an existing firm or a retiring contractor's clients
Gives clients and a name at once, but costs money; check its records, debts and reputation carefully first.

Example

Goals and milestones

Save J$900,000 for start-up costs within 36 months.
Niche and market
Who your customers are and why they would choose you.
Farmers and households in the parish needing reliable solar pumping.

Savings, a credit union loan and hire purchase for a van.

Illness, late payment, a large competitor.

The training, licences and support you need.
A solar PV course, a bookkeeping course, a mentor.

Every six months.

head: Year
Typical milestones
Why it matters
rows: Finish Level 3; start the process for the electrical licence the law requires for your work; save a fixed sum every month; keep a log of the jobs you do.
Without the licence you cannot legally sign for your own installations. Savings reduce what you must borrow later.
Widen your experience in the niche you want; learn estimating and pricing from your supervisor; take a short business or bookkeeping course.
Skill and accurate prices win work and protect profit.
Buy your own tools and test instruments a piece at a time, without debt; do small weekend jobs; build a list of clients and contacts.
You test the market cheaply and start to build a name.
Write the business plan and cash flow forecast; register the business with the Companies Office and TAJ; arrange insurance and a business bank account; talk to lenders about a van.
The firm is legal and ready, and the figures show what you need.
Leave employment with savings to cover at least three to six months of costs, the van in place and first clients and builders lined up; review the plan every six months.
You start with work and a cushion, not with debt and hope.

blocks.note: Talk to your family before you commit. Your plan affects their income, their savings and your time with them. A plan they understand and support is far more likely to succeed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Support, mentors and keeping up to date

ul: A **mentor** is an experienced contractor or business person who shares advice, contacts and lessons from their own mistakes. A mentor does not do your jobs, lend you money without terms or sign your certificates.
HEART/NSTA Trust and NCTVET offer further training and certification, including higher-level electrical and renewable energy courses.

Business support agencies such as the Jamaica Business Development Corporation (JBDC), credit unions and banks run small-business advice, training and loan programmes. Ask your instructor which are current.

Keep training. New markets keep opening (solar PV with batteries, electric vehicle (EV) chargers, energy-saving retrofits, smart controls), and codes and connection rules change. A contractor who stops learning loses work and may break new rules without knowing it.

blocks.p: Running a firm can mean 70-hour weeks. Tiredness causes mistakes, and in electrical work a tired mistake can kill. Plan rest days and holidays into the year as firmly as you plan jobs, keep time for your family, and arrange savings and insurance to cover illness: a one-person firm earns nothing while the owner is sick.

blocks.note: Never let deadlines or money worries push you into working live, skipping tests or cutting corners. One serious accident can end a small firm: injury, claims, a lost licence and a lost name.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Knowing yourself: skills audit, SWOT and SMART goals

blocks.p: Your strategy must start from a clear goal and an honest look at yourself. If you overrate your skills or your savings, the plan will fail at the first test.

head: Skill area
Rate yourself on
How to close a gap
rows: Technical
Installation, inspection and testing, fault-finding, reading drawings, the code, and your niche (such as solar PV or generators).
Courses, supervised experience, working beside a specialist.
Business and money
Estimating and pricing, bookkeeping, cash flow, tax and payroll.
A short business or bookkeeping course, an accountant, a mentor.
Selling and customer care
Explaining options to clients, writing quotations, handling complaints, meeting builders.
Practice, feedback from clients, preparing quotations with your supervisor.
Management
Planning jobs, ordering materials, supervising helpers, keeping to time.
Taking charge of small jobs and teams at work before you start on your own.
Personal
Self-discipline, health, time management, coping with stress and setbacks.
Routines, rest, and honest feedback from people you trust.

blocks.p: Rate each skill, for example from 1 to 5, and ask a supervisor or an experienced colleague to rate you too. Where the two ratings differ, find out why. The gaps become goals in your plan.

A **SWOT analysis** sorts what you know into four boxes. **Strengths** and **weaknesses** are **inside** you: your skills, money, habits and contacts. You can change them. **Opportunities** and **threats** are **outside** you: the market, the economy, the rules and the competition. You cannot control them, but you can prepare for them.

head: Box
Inside or outside?
Examples for an electrician planning a solar and generator business
rows: Strengths
Inside, helpful
Level 3 qualification
Three years installing solar PV with an employer
Good at fault-finding
A good name with past clients
No debts
Weaknesses
Inside, harmful
Little experience of pricing or bookkeeping
No vehicle
Small savings
Poor at following up enquiries
Opportunities
Outside, helpful
High electricity prices pushing homes and businesses towards solar
Outages and hurricanes raising demand for generators and changeover switches
Builders needing reliable subcontractors
New housing schemes in the parish
Threats
Outside, harmful
Larger solar firms with buying power
Cheap unlicensed workers
Changes in the rules for connecting systems to the grid
Panel and battery prices moving with the exchange rate
Slow-paying clients

blocks.note: A common mistake is to put outside things in the Strengths box ('demand for solar is high') or inside things in Threats ('I have no van'). Ask: is this about me, or about the world around me? 'I have no van' is a weakness; 'fuel prices are rising' is a threat.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Put together
Ask
Example action
rows: Strengths and opportunities
How can I use my strengths to grab this opportunity?

Weaknesses and opportunities
Which weakness stops me taking the opportunity, and how do I fix it?

Strengths and threats
How can my strengths protect me?
Compete on quality, certification and after-sales service, not on price against unlicensed workers.
Weaknesses and threats
Where am I most exposed, and how do I reduce it?
Build savings and insist on deposits, so that one slow payer cannot sink the firm.

blocks.p: A goal you cannot measure or date is only a wish. Write goals that are SMART.

head: Letter
Means
Test question
rows: S
Specific
Does it say exactly what will be done?
M
Measurable
Can it be counted or checked?

Is it possible with your skills, time and money?

head: Vague
SMART
rows: Save some money.
Save J$25,000 every month in a credit union account for 36 months, to reach J$900,000 for start-up costs.
Get more experience.
Lead the installation of at least eight grid-tied solar systems under my supervisor by the end of next year.

blocks.p: A **milestone** is a checkpoint that shows you are on track: licence obtained, J$450,000 saved, first van bought. Under each milestone, list the **actions**: the small tasks, each with a date. Review progress on set dates and adjust the plan when life changes. A plan that is never reviewed soon stops being followed.

sections.title: Finding a niche and researching the market

blocks.p: A **niche** is a narrow part of the market that you can serve better than others. A new contractor who offers 'all electrical work' competes with everybody, mostly on price. A niche lets you build deep skill, a name and contacts, with fewer rivals and fairer prices. You can still do general work, but your marketing leads with the niche. A niche still has competitors, and it still needs the right licences and permits.

head: Possible niche
Who buys
What it needs from you
rows: Solar PV, with or without batteries
Homeowners, small businesses, farms, schools
Solar training and experience; inverter and battery knowledge; the rules for connecting to the JPS grid; reliable suppliers.
Standby generators and changeover (transfer) switches
Homes, clinics, shops, churches, small hotels
Safe changeover wiring so a generator can never feed back into JPS lines; generator sizing; servicing.
Maintenance contracts
Hotels, factories, schools, apartment complexes, offices
Planned inspection and testing, emergency call-outs, good records and reliability.
Small commercial fit-outs
Shops, pharmacies, restaurants, offices in plazas
Reading drawings, working to a builder's programme, three-phase work, neat finishes.
Energy-saving retrofits
Businesses with high electricity bills
LED lighting, controls and load surveys, with clear figures on the savings.
EV charging points
Car dealers, businesses, homeowners with electric cars
Training on chargers, load calculations, dedicated circuits and protection.
Solar water pumping and farm work
Farmers, for example in St Elizabeth and Manchester
Pumps, motors, controls and outdoor wiring; travel to rural sites.

ul: People already pay for this work, or clearly need it.
Few good firms serve it in your area.
You have the skill, or can get it in your plan's time.
Customers can afford a fair price.
There is enough of it to keep you busy all year, not for one season.
It fits your strengths and your vision.

blocks.p: **Market research** means collecting facts about customers, competitors and demand before you spend money. **Primary research** is information you gather yourself. **Secondary research** is information other people have already published.

head: Method
Kind
What you learn
rows: Talking to hardware and electrical stores
Primary
What contractors are buying, which work is growing and who is busy.
Talking to builders, architects, property managers and hotel engineers
Primary
Whether they need another contractor, what they pay and what frustrates them about the ones they use.
A short survey of possible customers (not only friends and family)
Primary
Whether they would buy, how often and at what price.
Studying at least three competitors: services, prices, reviews and how fast they respond
Primary
Gaps you could fill and the prices the market accepts.
News and reports on energy prices, building approvals, housing schemes and tourism projects
Secondary
Whether demand is growing or shrinking.

blocks.note: Asking family and friends whether they like your idea is not market research. They want to encourage you and may never buy. Ask people who would actually pay: what they buy now, how often, from whom and for how much. Copying a competitor's price list is not research either: you do not know their costs.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **unique selling point** is the clear reason a customer should choose you rather than a competitor. It must be something customers value, something competitors do not do well, and something you can deliver every time.

head: Weak USP
Strong USP
rows: 'Cheapest in town.' Someone will always undercut you, and low prices destroy profit.
Licensed, tested and certified work, with a written one-year warranty.
'A smart van and logo.' It looks good but solves no customer's problem.
Emergency call-out within three hours anywhere in the parish.
'A big-sounding name.' Customers soon find out how big you are.
Solar systems sized from your own JPS bills, with a written estimate of the savings.

blocks.h: Testing the idea before you jump

ul: Do a few paid jobs in the niche at weekends, with your employer's knowledge where your contract requires it.
Record the true time and cost of each, so you know the real profit.
Ask each client for honest feedback, and note how they heard of you.
Check that enquiries keep coming without you chasing every one.

blocks.p: A legal set-up protects you, your clients and your workers, and builders, lenders and public bodies will ask for proof of it before they give you work or money.

Before you advertise or take on installation work in your own name, make sure you hold the **licence the law requires** for the work you will do and certify. In Jamaica, new and altered installations must be inspected and certified before JPS will connect them, under the oversight of the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)**. Find out from the GER and your instructor which licence applies to the work in your plan and how long it takes to get, and put it early in your five-year plan.

blocks.note: A business name, a logo and a website do not make you a legal contractor. The licence comes first.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Structure
What it means
Points to know
rows: Sole trader
You own and run the business alone, in your own name or a registered business name.
Easiest and cheapest to set up, and you keep all the profit. You are **personally liable** for all its debts: your savings, car or home could be taken to pay them.
Partnership
Two or more people own the business together and share the profit.
Shares cost, skills and work. Each partner is usually liable for all the firm's debts, including those run up by the other partner. Write a partnership agreement first.
Limited liability company
The company is a separate legal 'person' that owns the business; the owners hold shares and are usually its directors.

The owners' own assets are protected (**limited liability**): they risk what they put in. Lenders often ask directors for a personal guarantee, which removes that protection for that loan. More paperwork: annual returns and proper accounts.

blocks.p: Agree everything in writing before you start, not by handshake. The agreement should say:

ul: what each partner puts in: money, a van, tools;
how profits and losses are shared, and how much each may draw each month;
who does what, and who may sign cheques, orders and contracts;
what happens if a partner wants to leave, falls ill or dies;
how disagreements will be settled.

flow: Register the business name, or form the company, at the Companies Office of Jamaica (COJ)
Register with Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ): a company gets its own TRN; a sole trader uses their own TRN
Open a separate business bank account and keep business and personal money apart
Register for GCT if your taxable sales reach the threshold TAJ sets; then charge it at the current rate and file returns
Register as an employer (NIS, NHT, education tax, HEART/NSTA Trust) before you hire anyone
Keep records from day one: every sale, every purchase, every receipt

blocks.p: COJ's business registration forms can usually make several of these registrations in one application. Ask COJ or your instructor for the current forms and fees.

ul: **GCT (General Consumption Tax)** is charged on most goods and services. Only a business **registered for GCT** may charge it.

A registered business charges GCT on its sales and can usually claim back the GCT it pays on business purchases, but only with proper supplier invoices. That is one reason to keep every supplier invoice.
Show GCT as a **separate line** on quotations and invoices, at the current rate, so the client sees the price before tax, the tax and the total.
As a self-employed person you pay income tax on your profit, pay your own NIS, NHT and education tax contributions, and file a yearly return. An accountant can set this up with you.
Public bodies and many large clients ask for a **tax compliance certificate (TCC)** from TAJ before they award a contract. You can get one only if your tax affairs are up to date.

head: Insurance
What it covers
Why an electrical firm needs it
rows: Public liability
Injury to other people, or damage to their property, caused by your work.
A fire from a loose connection, or a client tripping over your cable, could bring a claim far bigger than the job. Builders and hotels often ask for proof of it.
Employer's liability (workers' compensation)
Your own workers injured at work.
Electrical work carries real risks of shock, burns and falls.
Motor vehicle
The van, other road users and their property.
Third-party motor insurance is required by law; comprehensive cover protects your van.
Tools and equipment ('all risks')
Theft of, or damage to, tools and test instruments on site and in the van.
Test instruments are costly, and without them you cannot certify work.
Contract works
Damage to the work itself before handover.
Often asked for on larger building contracts.
Health, disability or income cover for the owner
Your medical costs, and income while you cannot work.
A one-person firm earns nothing while the owner is ill.

blocks.note: Insurance does not pay for poor workmanship, and it does not replace a licence. Read what each policy leaves out.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Invoice every job correctly and record all income. 'Cash, no invoice, no GCT' is tax evasion, and it leaves you with no records to show a lender.
Never skip or 'arrange' an electrical inspection, even when a client asks you to save time. Explain that it is required and arrange it.
Never make or advise an illegal connection to JPS lines.
Take only work you are licensed, skilled and equipped to do safely. Bring in a specialist or turn the rest down.
Use the materials you quoted, and tell the client about any change before you make it.
Pay workers, suppliers and taxes on time.
Keep clients' information private, and never take a former employer's clients or price lists.

blocks.note: In a small island, word travels fast, good and bad. Your name is your most valuable asset.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A contractor who does not know the true cost of a job cannot price it. Most new firms that fail on money were busy: they simply charged less than their work cost them.

head: Kind
What it is
Examples
rows: Direct costs
Costs that belong to one particular job.
Cable, breakers, panels, fittings and conduit for that job; labour hours on it; a scissor lift hired for it.
Overheads (indirect costs)
Costs of running the business that cannot be charged to one job.
Insurance, office phone and data, the accountant, advertising, van costs, licence fees, tool replacement, test-instrument calibration, your own time on quotes and paperwork.
Fixed costs
Stay the same however much work you do, in the short term.
Rent, insurance, loan repayments, van licence and registration, software subscriptions.
Variable costs
Rise and fall with the amount of work.
Materials, fuel for site visits, hourly paid helpers.

blocks.note: Direct or indirect is about whether a cost belongs to a job. Fixed or variable is about whether it changes with the amount of work. Most overheads are fixed and most direct costs are variable, but not all.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Tools, test instruments and vans lose value as they are used. **Depreciation** spreads that loss over their useful life, so each year's costs, and your charge-out rate, carry a fair share of it. The simplest method is **straight-line depreciation**:
**Depreciation per year = (cost − value at the end of its life) ÷ years of life**

Example: a multifunction tester costs J$480,000 and should last 8 years, with no value at the end. Depreciation = 480,000 ÷ 8 = **J$60,000 a year**. If your prices do not include it, there will be no money to replace the tester when it wears out.
A **charge-out rate** is the price you charge for each hour of labour. It must cover your wage **and** all the overheads, not just what you used to earn as an employee.

flow: Decide the yearly wage you need
Add up the yearly overheads, including depreciation
Work out the realistic chargeable hours
Divide (wage + overheads) by the chargeable hours
Add profit
Check the result against the market

head: Line
Worked example
rows: Wage the owner needs
Overheads, including depreciation of the van and instruments
Total to recover
Working hours: about 46 weeks × 40 hours, after holidays and sick days
about 1,840 hours
Less hours that cannot be charged: travel, quoting, buying, paperwork, rain days, gaps between jobs
about 340 hours
Chargeable hours
1,500 hours
Rate before profit: 4,350,000 ÷ 1,500
J$2,900 an hour

blocks.note: Why new contractors set the rate too low: they compare it with their old wage; they forget overheads and depreciation; they count every working hour as chargeable; they forget their own holidays and sick days; or they try to undercut everyone. The result is a firm that is busy but broke.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Building up the price of a job

flow: Take-off: list every material from the drawings or a site survey
Price the materials from current supplier quotes, plus a small allowance for waste
Estimate the hours for each task and multiply by the charge-out rate
Add other direct costs: equipment hire, permits, travel to remote sites
Add a contingency for risks you can foresee but not measure
Add profit as a mark-up on the total cost
Add GCT at the current rate, on a separate line, if you are registered
Check the price against the market and your past jobs

head: Line
Amount (J$)
rows: Materials from the take-off, at current prices
Waste allowance, 5% of materials
Labour: 28 hours × J$3,000 (the rate before profit)
Scissor-lift hire, 2 days
Total direct cost
Contingency, 5% (old building, hidden faults likely)
Cost including contingency
Mark-up for profit, 15%
Price before GCT
GCT
At the current rate, on a separate line (if registered)

blocks.note: Count overheads and profit **once**. Here labour is costed at the rate before profit, and profit is added once at the end. Some firms cost labour at a bare wage and add overheads as a separate percentage instead; either works, as long as nothing is left out or counted twice.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Mark-up** is profit as a percentage of **cost**. **Margin** (profit margin) is profit as a percentage of the **selling price**. They describe the same profit, so the margin is always the smaller figure.

ul: Mark-up % = profit ÷ cost × 100
Margin % = profit ÷ price × 100
Price for a target margin = cost ÷ (1 − margin as a decimal)

blocks.p: Example: LED fittings cost the firm J$60,000 and are resold with a 50% mark-up. Price = 60,000 × 1.5 = J$90,000. Profit = J$30,000. Mark-up = 30,000 ÷ 60,000 = **50%**. Margin = 30,000 ÷ 90,000 = **33.3%**.

blocks.note: To reach a target margin, do not add the margin percentage to the cost. A 20% margin needs a 25% mark-up: price = cost ÷ 0.80. Adding 20% to the cost gives a margin of only about 16.7%.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Gross profit** = sales − the direct costs of the jobs (materials and direct labour). It shows whether the jobs themselves are priced well. **Net profit** = gross profit − overheads. It shows whether the business as a whole makes money. A firm can make a good gross profit on every job and still make a net loss if overheads are too high or there are too few jobs.

head: Line
A year's figures (J$)
rows: Sales
Less direct costs of the jobs
Gross profit
Less overheads
Net profit (before tax)

sections.title: Break-even, start-up money and cash flow

blocks.p: The **break-even point** is the amount of work at which income exactly covers all costs: no profit, no loss. Below it you lose money; above it each job adds profit. Working it out before you start tells you how much work you must win each month, and whether your plan is realistic.
Each job leaves a **contribution** towards the fixed costs: **contribution = price − the job's variable costs**.
**Break-even (number of jobs) = fixed costs ÷ contribution per job**

Example: fixed costs are J$360,000 a month. A typical service call-out is charged at J$18,000 and has J$6,000 of variable costs, so each leaves J$12,000. Break-even = 360,000 ÷ 12,000 = **30 call-outs a month**.

blocks.note: If the answer is not a whole number, round **up**. If the sum gives 27.3 jobs, you need 28 to cover your costs.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: List everything you must buy or pay for before the first client pays you, and show where the money will come from.

head: Item
Example (J$)
rows: Used van, with licence and registration
Hand and power tools
Test instruments: multifunction tester, clamp meter, voltage tester
PPE and ladders
Insurance for the first year
Registration, licence and professional fees
Van signs, flyers and a social media page
Opening stock of common materials
Working capital: cash for the first three months' costs
**Total**

blocks.p: Paid for by: own savings J$1,900,000 (including a J$400,000 deposit on the van); hire purchase on the van J$2,400,000; a credit union loan J$1,200,000. Total J$5,500,000.

blocks.note: Lenders like to see the owner put in a fair share of their own money. It shows commitment and reduces the loan.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Ways to pay for the start

head: Source
Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Own savings
No interest or repayments; shows commitment.
Takes years to build; your own money is at risk.
Family and friends
Flexible; may charge little or no interest.
Can damage relationships if things go wrong; write the terms down anyway.
Credit union loan
Members often get fair rates; local and personal.
Usually needs savings with the credit union and a record as a member.
Bank loan
Larger sums, with a set repayment plan.
Needs a business plan, a cash flow forecast and collateral or a guarantor; interest; repayments start at once.
Hire purchase (HP)
Use the van or equipment now and pay in instalments; you own it after the last one.
Costs more in total than paying cash; it can be taken back if you fall behind.
Leasing
Use equipment for a monthly fee, with little paid at the start.
You never own it; usually dearer in the long run.
Supplier credit
Buy materials now and pay later, for example in 30 days.
Must be earned with a good record; lost if you pay late.
Overdraft
A buffer for short gaps in cash.
High interest; the bank can reduce or withdraw it; not for buying a van.

blocks.note: Match the finance to what it pays for. A van, which lasts years, suits a longer loan or hire purchase. A short gap in cash suits an overdraft or supplier credit. Buying the van, tools and instruments all on short-term credit means high repayments that drain your cash in the first months, before the work comes in.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Profit** is counted when work is done and invoiced. **Cash** arrives only when the client pays. On a large job you buy materials and pay wages weeks or months before you are paid, so a profitable firm can still run out of cash and fail. The usual cause is clients who are slow to pay their invoices.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Debtors (accounts receivable)
Customers who owe the business money for work already invoiced.
Creditors (accounts payable)
Suppliers and others the business owes money to.
Working capital
The money tied up in stock, debtors and cash, less what the business owes in the short term. It keeps the business running from day to day.
Retention
A small share of the contract price, often 5% to 10%, that the client holds back until the defects period ends and any defects are put right.
Deposit
Money paid before work starts, usually enough to buy the first materials.
Stage payment
A payment due when an agreed stage of the job is finished.

blocks.p: A **cash flow forecast** is a table of the money you expect to come in (receipts) and go out (payments) each month, usually for at least the next 12 months. It shows a shortage in advance, so you can act before it happens.

head: Line (J$)
Month 1
Month 2
Month 3
rows: Opening balance
Receipts: deposits and stage payments
Payments: materials
Payments: wages and owner's drawings
Payments: overheads and loan repayment
Closing balance

blocks.p: **Closing balance = opening balance + receipts − payments**, and each month's closing balance is the next month's opening balance. Month 2 shows a shortfall of J$30,000. Seeing it now, the owner can act: invoice the next stage the day it is finished, delay a purchase, or agree an overdraft in advance.

ul: Take a **deposit** before you start, enough to cover the first materials.
Agree **stage payments** in the written contract, tied to clear stages such as first fix, second fix, and testing and handover.
Buy materials in stages, as the job needs them, and use supplier credit where you have it, so you pay suppliers after the client pays you.
Invoice promptly and accurately, and follow up late payers politely but firmly.
Check a new client before giving credit, and never let one client owe you more than you can afford to lose.
Keep the forecast up to date, and keep a buffer: savings or an overdraft agreed before you need it.
Do not take on more large jobs at once than you can fund until the clients pay.

blocks.h: The business plan and the lender

blocks.p: A **business plan** is the written form of your strategy, with the figures. You use it to run the business and to persuade lenders and partners. What a lender most wants to see is a sound plan with realistic cash flow figures.

head: Section
What it contains
What it tells a lender
rows: Summary
The business, the niche, the loan wanted and what it is for.
What is being asked, at a glance.
The owner
Qualifications, licence, experience and the people involved.
Whether you can do the work and run a firm.
The market
Customers, competitors, demand and your USP.
Whether there is enough work at a fair price.
Operations
Services, equipment, suppliers, premises and staff plans.
Whether you can deliver the work.
Marketing
How you will find clients and set prices.
Whether the sales forecast is believable.
Financial plan
Start-up costs and how they are funded, including your own money; sales forecast; cash flow forecast for at least 12 months; break-even; projected profit and loss.
Whether the loan can be repaid, and when.
Risks
The main risks and what you will do about each.
That you have planned ahead.

blocks.note: In a loan meeting, know your key figures without reading them: your break-even point, your charge-out rate and the lowest month in your cash flow. Be open about risks: a lender trusts an owner who has seen the problems coming.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Winning work: marketing, quotations and contracts

blocks.p: **Marketing** is everything you do to make the right customers know about you, trust you and choose you. Start from your USP, then choose the methods that reach your niche.

head: Customer group
Methods that work
Points to know
rows: Homeowners
Word of mouth and referrals; online reviews; a social media page with photos of neat work; signs on the van; cards and flyers at hardware stores.
Reply to messages quickly. Ask every satisfied client to recommend you and to leave a review.
Builders, architects and engineers
Visiting sites and building suppliers; meeting contractors; fast, clear quotations; reliable first jobs.
One builder who trusts you can give you years of repeat work.
Businesses, hotels and institutions
Maintenance contracts; tenders; meeting the maintenance manager or hotel engineer.
Steady income. They expect records, certificates and a quick response.
Public bodies
Tenders under the government's procurement rules.
Read every requirement; documents such as a tax compliance certificate are usually needed, and late or incomplete bids are rejected.

blocks.note: Track where each enquiry comes from: a referral, the van sign, social media, a builder. Spend more on what brings paying work and stop what does not.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Compete on value, not only on price

blocks.p: Being the cheapest on every job is a weak strategy. Someone will always undercut you, and low prices leave nothing for tools, insurance, mistakes or growth. Compete on what customers value: reliability, safety, certified work, clean sites, clear communication and after-sales service. Price fairly, explain what the client gets for the money, and turn down work that cannot be done safely at the price offered.

head: Document
What it is
rows: Estimate
A rough guide to the likely cost. It is not binding.
Quotation
A fixed-price offer for a clearly defined job. Once the client accepts it, it can form a contract.
Tender (bid)
A priced offer sent in competition with other firms, usually for a large job from a builder or a public body, following the client's rules and deadline.

ul: Your business name and contact details; the client's name and the site address; the date and a quotation number.
**Scope**: exactly what work is included, with quantities and the standard of materials, for example '12 duplex outlets, 20 A, on 12 AWG cable'.
**Exclusions**: what is not included, such as cutting chases and making good, painting, JPS fees or work by other trades.
**Price**: the total before tax, GCT on a separate line at the current rate (if you are registered) and the total.
**Payment terms**: deposit, stage payments and when the balance is due.
**Programme**: the start date and how long the work will take.
**Validity**: how long the price stands, for example 30 days, because material prices change.
The warranty, how variations will be handled, and a place for the client to sign and accept.

blocks.p: For anything beyond a small job, agree a **written contract**: the accepted quotation plus the terms (scope, price, stage payments, programme, retention, warranty and how disputes are settled). A written contract with staged payments is the best protection against a client who will not pay a large final bill.

A **variation** is a change to the agreed work, such as extra outlets or different fittings. Before you do it, write down the change, its price and any extra time, and get the client's written agreement. Do not do extra work free 'to keep the client happy', and never fit it first and send a surprise bill afterwards.

flow: Listen without arguing
Thank the client and apologise for the problem
Check the facts
Offer to put it right, and agree what and when
Do it, then follow up
Change whatever caused it

blocks.p: Answer a bad online review calmly and politely, offer to put things right, and continue the conversation privately. Never post an angry reply and never post fake reviews: other customers judge you by how you handle complaints.

**Repeat business** and referrals cost far less to win than new customers. Leave every site clean, explain the work and the certificate, follow up a week later, remind clients when testing or servicing is due, and offer maintenance contracts.

sections.title: Running and growing the firm: records, staff, risk and review

head: Record
What it holds
Why
rows: A job file for each job
Enquiry, quotation, acceptance, variations, orders, delivery notes, hours worked, test results and certificates, invoices and payments.
Shows the true profit on each job, gives evidence in a dispute, and helps you price the next one.
Sales and purchase records
Every invoice you send and every supplier invoice you receive, with the GCT on each.
Tax and GCT returns, chasing debts and paying suppliers.
Bank and cash records
Bank statements, receipts and a petty cash book.
Shows where the money went, and catches errors and theft.
Petty cash
A small sum kept for small purchases, with a voucher and receipt for each.
Small items, such as a box of wire connectors, are still business costs.
Payroll records
Hours, wages, deductions and payments to TAJ.
Required by law once you employ staff.
Asset register
Tools, instruments and vehicles, with cost, date, serial number and calibration dates.
Insurance claims, depreciation and calibration.

blocks.p: Accounting software, or a simple spreadsheet kept up to date, shows quickly what you are owed, what you owe, your profit and the tax due. It does not replace receipts: keep the originals or scanned copies, and keep them for as long as TAJ requires.

head: Statement
What it shows
rows: Profit and loss account (income statement)
Sales, costs, gross profit and net profit over a period, such as a year.
Balance sheet (statement of financial position)
What the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owner's equity, on one date.
Cash flow forecast
Expected receipts and payments month by month, and the bank balance they lead to.

blocks.p: Hire your first worker when your records show steady work (jobs turned away or delayed) and cash flow that can pay a wage every week, even in a slow month, and when the forecast shows that the extra work will more than cover the wage and its costs. Many owners grow in steps: subcontract to a trusted licensed electrician, take on an apprentice or a part-time helper, and only then hire full-time staff. Write a job description, choose fairly, and check qualifications and references.

ul: Give a written contract or written terms of employment, and pay at least the national minimum wage.

Deduct the employee's income tax (PAYE), NIS, NHT and education tax from their pay, add the employer's own contributions (including the HEART/NSTA Trust contribution where it applies) and pay them to TAJ on time, with the monthly and yearly returns.
Keep payroll records and give a payslip with each payment.
Provide a safe workplace, training, PPE and supervision. Never leave an unqualified worker to work alone on installations.
Arrange employer's liability insurance.
Give staff the holidays, sick leave and other rights that employment law provides, and treat them with respect.
Remember that you are now a leader: planning the work and checking quality take time away from doing the work yourself.

blocks.p: Taking on many big jobs at once can feel like success. But materials and wages must be paid long before clients pay, quality slips when the owner cannot supervise every site, and one slow payer can sink the firm. Grow at the pace your cash, your people and your supervision can support.

head: Risk
How the owner reduces it
rows: Late payment or non-payment
Written contracts, deposits, stage payments, checking new clients, prompt invoicing and follow-up.
Pricing too low
Careful take-offs, a proper charge-out rate, contingency, and comparing each job's estimate with its actual cost.
An accident or a fault that injures someone or damages property
Safe isolation, inspection and testing, trained and supervised staff, refusing work beyond your skills or equipment, public liability insurance.
The owner ill or injured
Savings, health and income insurance, and a trusted electrician who can cover.
Theft of tools, instruments or the van
Lock up, mark tools, keep an asset register, insure.
Material prices rising
Short quotation validity, current supplier quotes, price-review terms on long jobs.
Too little work in a slow period
A spread of clients, maintenance contracts, more than one service.
Changes in rules or technology
Keep training; follow updates from the GER, JPS and the code.

blocks.p: Write the risks in a simple **risk register**, rate each one by how likely it is and how serious it would be, deal with the biggest first, and review the list regularly.

Compare actual results with the plan at least every three to six months. When results fall short, first find out why: is it price, marketing, the niche, the economy or your own time? Then adjust the plan. Do not react in panic: closing at once, doubling prices or stopping your records all make things worse.

head: Measure
What it tells you
rows: Sales against the forecast
Whether demand is what you expected.
Profit on each finished job, estimate against actual
Whether your pricing and estimating work.
Quotations won ÷ quotations sent
Whether your prices and follow-up are right. Winning almost every quote often means you are too cheap.
Money owed by clients, and for how long
Whether you are being paid on time.
Repeat and referred clients
Whether customers are satisfied.
Call-backs and defects
Whether quality is slipping.
Hours worked by the owner
Whether the pace can be kept up safely.
Cash balance against the forecast
Whether a shortfall is coming.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain what a personal entrepreneurial strategy is and what it contains.
I can compare working as an employee with running a business, and name the routes into business for an electrician.
I can carry out a skills audit and a personal SWOT analysis, putting each item in the right box.
I can use a SWOT to decide what to build on, what to fix and what to prepare for.
I can write SMART goals and a five-year plan with yearly milestones.
I can choose a niche, carry out market research and state a strong USP.
I can explain the licence, registration, tax and insurance steps for an electrical firm in Jamaica, and why each matters.
I can compare a sole trader, a partnership and a limited company.
I can separate direct costs, overheads, fixed and variable costs, and work out straight-line depreciation.
I can work out a charge-out rate and explain why many new contractors set it too low.
I can build up the price of a job with materials, labour, contingency, profit and GCT on a separate line.
I can work out mark-up, margin, gross profit and net profit, and tell mark-up from margin.
I can work out a break-even point.
I can prepare a start-up budget and choose suitable sources of finance.
I can explain why a profitable firm can run out of cash, and build and use a cash flow forecast.
I can describe what a lender expects in a business plan.
I can plan marketing for homeowners, builders and businesses, and handle a complaint.
I can write a quotation, explain tenders, contracts, variations and retention.
I can list the records to keep and my duties as an employer.
I can list the main risks to a new firm with their controls, and review the strategy against results.

head: Quantity
Formula
rows: Straight-line depreciation per year
(cost − end value) ÷ years of life
Charge-out rate before profit
(wage + overheads) ÷ chargeable hours
Mark-up %
profit ÷ cost × 100
Margin %
profit ÷ price × 100
Price for a target margin
cost ÷ (1 − margin)
Contribution per job
price − variable costs of the job
Break-even number of jobs
fixed costs ÷ contribution per job, rounded up
Gross profit
sales − direct costs
Net profit
gross profit − overheads
Closing cash balance
opening balance + receipts − payments

terms: Balance sheet
A statement of what a business owns, what it owes and the owner's equity, on one date.
Break-even point
The amount of work at which income exactly covers all costs, with no profit or loss.
Business plan
The written strategy and figures for a business, used to run it and to persuade lenders and partners.
Cash flow forecast
A month-by-month table of expected receipts, payments and bank balance.
Charge-out rate
The price charged for each hour of labour, covering wages, overheads and profit.
Collateral
Something of value, such as property, pledged to a lender as security for a loan.
Contingency
An amount added to a price for risks that can be foreseen but not measured.
Contribution
What a job leaves towards fixed costs: its price less its variable costs.
Creditors
People and firms the business owes money to; accounts payable.
Debtors
Customers who owe the business money for work already invoiced; accounts receivable.
Depreciation
The loss in value of tools, instruments and vehicles, spread over their useful life.
Direct cost
A cost that belongs to one particular job, such as its materials and labour.
Entrepreneur
A person who spots an opportunity, takes a measured risk and organises resources to build a business.
GCT
General Consumption Tax, charged by registered businesses at the current rate and shown as a separate line.
Gross profit
Sales less the direct costs of the jobs.
Limited liability
The protection of a company's owners, who risk only what they put into the company.
Margin
Profit as a percentage of the selling price.
Mark-up
Profit as a percentage of cost.
Mentor
An experienced person who shares advice, contacts and experience.
Milestone
A dated checkpoint in a plan that shows progress.
Net profit
Gross profit less overheads: the profit left after all costs.
Niche
A narrow part of the market that a firm can serve better than others.
NIS
National Insurance Scheme: a contribution deducted from wages, with an employer's share, and also paid by the self-employed.
Overheads
Costs of running the business that cannot be charged to one job; indirect costs.
Petty cash
A small amount of money kept for small purchases, with a voucher for each.
Public liability insurance
Insurance that covers injury or damage the business causes to other people or their property.
Quotation
A fixed-price offer for a defined job.
Repeat business
Work from past clients who come back again and again.
Retention
A share of the contract price held back by the client until defects are put right.
SMART goal
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Sole trader
A person who owns and runs a business alone and is personally liable for its debts.
SWOT analysis
A review of strengths and weaknesses (inside) and opportunities and threats (outside).
Tender
A priced offer sent in competition with other firms for a job.
Unique selling point (USP)
The clear reason a customer should choose your firm rather than a competitor.
Variation
A change to the agreed work, priced and agreed in writing before it is done.
Working capital
The money tied up in stock, debtors and cash, less short-term debts, that keeps a business running day to day.

c1.title: Rushane's five-year plan in Santa Cruz
c1.text: Rushane Bryan, 27, is a Level 3 electrician with a contractor in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. He has helped to install over 30 solar systems but has never priced a job, and he has no vehicle. Farmers near Santa Cruz keep asking him about solar-powered irrigation pumps, and two big solar firms from Mandeville and Black River already work in the parish. He wants his own firm within five years. Before he leaves his job he wants savings equal to six months of his household costs, which are J$120,000 a month. He has J$350,000 saved.

c2.title: Tamika's charge-out rate in Lucea
c2.text: Tamika Lewis runs a one-van electrical firm in Lucea, Hanover. She wants to pay herself J$2,400,000 a year. Her other yearly overheads (insurance, fuel and repairs, phone and data, tools and calibration, accountant and advertising) come to J$1,300,000. She bought the van for J$3,000,000 and expects to sell it for J$500,000 after five years. She works about 2,000 hours a year, but travel, quoting, buying materials and paperwork take up about 600 of them, and she cannot charge clients for those hours.

c3.title: A pharmacy rewire in Christiana
c3.text: Kerry-Ann Thompson's firm in Christiana, Manchester, is quoting to rewire and relight a pharmacy. Her take-off gives J$210,000 of materials at current prices. She allows 36 labour hours at J$2,500 an hour, although her own sums give a charge-out rate of J$3,000 an hour before profit. The building is old, so she adds a 5% contingency to the total cost, then a 20% mark-up. The owner's own mason will cut the chases in the walls and make good afterwards.

c4.title: A hotel maintenance contract in Negril
c4.text: Andrea Campbell and Kirk Dawkins own an electrical company in Negril, Westmoreland. They have won a one-year maintenance contract with a hotel, invoiced at J$200,000 at the end of each month. The hotel pays each invoice 60 days later (the month 1 invoice is paid in month 3, and so on) and holds back 5% of each payment as retention until the contract ends. Wages, materials and overheads for the contract cost J$150,000 a month, paid in the same month. They have J$100,000 in the bank for the contract when it starts.

c5.title: Three years on in Port Maria
c5.text: Omari Reid has run his electrical firm in Port Maria, St Mary, for three years, alone except for a helper on busy days. His records for the last 12 months show sales 30% above his plan, 14 enquiries turned away for lack of time, and a bank balance that never fell below two months of costs. Maintenance contracts gave 40% of his profit from 20% of his hours. He works about 70 hours a week, and last week his own testing found that he had reversed the polarity of an outlet on a new job. He wins 19 of every 20 quotations he sends.

questions.q: In Rushane's personal SWOT analysis, which item belongs in the Threats box?
o: His lack of experience in pricing and estimating
Having no vehicle of his own for tools and stock
Two big solar firms already working in the parish
Farmers asking about solar-powered irrigation pumps
questions.why: Threats are outside him and harmful: he cannot control competitors, but he can plan for them. His pricing gap and the missing vehicle are weaknesses (inside him), and the farmers' interest is an opportunity.

questions.q: From now on Rushane can save J$20,000 a month. How long will it take him to reach his savings target?
o: 19 months
36 months
18 months
6 months
questions.why: Target = 6 × J$120,000 = J$720,000. He still needs 720,000 − 350,000 = J$370,000. At J$20,000 a month that is 18.5 months, so he needs 19: after 18 months he would still be J$10,000 short. 36 months forgets the J$350,000 he already has.

questions.q: Which of these would be the best SMART goal for Rushane's first year?
o: Learn as much as he can about pricing over the coming year
Become the best-known solar installer in St Elizabeth
Open his own solar firm this year, to compete with the big firms
Price ten real jobs with his supervisor checking, by December
questions.why: It is specific (pricing real jobs), measurable (ten), achievable with help, relevant to his biggest weakness, and dated. 'As much as he can' cannot be checked, and opening this year ignores his lack of savings, vehicle and pricing skill.

questions.q: Which niche do Rushane's strengths and the local demand point to most clearly?
o: General house wiring, priced below the two big solar firms
Solar water pumping for farms, building on his solar work
Shop fit-outs in Kingston, where most building work is done
EV chargers, as electric cars will soon be common locally
questions.why: A good niche joins real local demand (farmers asking about solar pumps) to a strength he already has (solar installs). Competing on price for general work, moving to a distant market or betting on demand that does not yet exist locally are all weaker choices.

questions.q: Using the straight-line method, what yearly cost should Tamika include in her overheads for the van's loss of value?
questions.why: Depreciation = (cost − value at the end) ÷ years = (3,000,000 − 500,000) ÷ 5 = J$500,000 a year. J$600,000 ignores what she will get back when she sells the van.

questions.q: What must Tamika charge for each chargeable hour just to cover her own pay and all her overheads?
o: J$2,100 an hour
J$2,643 an hour
J$1,850 an hour
J$3,000 an hour
questions.why: Total to recover = 2,400,000 + 1,300,000 + 500,000 depreciation = J$4,200,000. Chargeable hours = 2,000 − 600 = 1,400. Rate = 4,200,000 ÷ 1,400 = J$3,000 an hour, before profit. Leaving out depreciation gives J$2,643; dividing by all 2,000 hours gives J$2,100.

questions.q: A friend tells Tamika to divide by all 2,000 hours, because 'every hour you work should be paid for'. What would happen if she did?
o: Her rate would be too low to recover all her costs
Her rate would be too high and she would lose work
Her rate would not change, as her overheads are the same
Her rate would be lower, but extra jobs would fill the gap
questions.why: Dividing by 2,000 gives J$2,100 an hour, but she can bill only about 1,400 hours: 1,400 × 2,100 = J$2,940,000, which is J$1,260,000 short of the J$4,200,000 she must recover. She has no spare hours for extra jobs; the hours she cannot bill must be paid for by the hours she can.

questions.q: A client complains that Tamika's hourly rate is far more than an electrician's wage. Which explanation is right?
o: The rate is set for all contractors by the Government Electrical Regulator
The rate includes GCT, which is always hidden in the labour charge
The rate also pays for her van, insurance, tools and unbillable hours
The rate is high because she is the only electrician working in Lucea
questions.why: An employee's wage is only part of a contractor's cost. Her rate must also cover overheads, depreciation and the hours she cannot bill, plus a fair profit. No regulator sets contractors' rates, and GCT, where charged, is shown as a separate line, not hidden.

questions.q: What price should Kerry-Ann's quotation show before GCT?
questions.why: Cost = 210,000 + (36 × 2,500) = J$300,000. Contingency: 5% of 300,000 = 15,000, giving J$315,000. Mark-up: 20% of 315,000 = 63,000, giving J$378,000. Adding 25% to J$300,000 in one step gives J$375,000, which leaves the contingency without its mark-up.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann tells her partner that her profit margin on this job is 20%. Is she right?
o: Yes: mark-up and margin are two names for one percentage
No: a 20% mark-up gives a margin of about 16.7%
No: the contingency counts as profit, so the margin is 25%
Yes: on small jobs the margin is the same as the mark-up
questions.why: Mark-up is profit on cost; margin is profit on price. Profit is J$63,000 and the price J$378,000, so the margin is 63,000 ÷ 378,000 ≈ 16.7%. The contingency is not profit: it is there to pay for hidden problems in the old building.

questions.q: How should the quotation deal with the cutting of chases and the making good of the walls?
o: Leave it out, as only electrical work goes on a quotation
Include it in her price, then pay the mason from the total
List it under exclusions, as work by the owner's own mason
Explain it to the owner by phone, to keep the quotation short
questions.why: Exclusions state clearly what is not included, so there is no argument later about who cuts chases, makes good or paints. Leaving it unsaid, or agreeing it only by phone, invites a dispute; pricing work someone else is doing wastes the client's money.

questions.q: Her own sums give a charge-out rate of J$3,000 an hour before profit. What is the effect of pricing the labour at J$2,500?
o: Her hours will not fully pay for her wage and overheads
The job will make more profit, as her labour costs less
None, as the 20% mark-up will cover the difference
The client pays less GCT, which balances out the loss
questions.why: The charge-out rate is what each hour must earn to cover her wage and overheads. At J$2,500 she recovers J$500 an hour too little: 36 × 500 = J$18,000 on this job, which comes straight out of her profit. Win work on value, not by pricing labour below its cost.

questions.q: If this contract were their only work, at the end of which month would the company's bank balance be lowest?
o: Month 1, at J$50,000 overdrawn
Month 2, at J$200,000 overdrawn
Month 3, at J$160,000 overdrawn
Month 4, at J$120,000 overdrawn
questions.why: Month 1: 100,000 − 150,000 = −50,000. Month 2: nothing received yet, so −50,000 − 150,000 = −200,000. From month 3 the hotel pays J$190,000 a month (J$200,000 less 5% retention) against J$150,000 out, so the balance climbs by J$40,000 a month. The contract makes a profit, yet it needs J$200,000 of cash the company does not have.

questions.q: What is the best way for Andrea and Kirk to deal with the cash gap in the first months?
o: Pay staff and suppliers late until the hotel's money arrives
Turn the contract down, since it loses money at the start
Use the GCT collected from other clients to cover the gap
Agree an overdraft with the bank before the contract starts
questions.why: The contract is profitable; the problem is timing. A buffer arranged before it is needed (an overdraft, savings, or an early payment agreed with the hotel) covers it. Paying staff and suppliers late breaks trust and may break the law, and GCT collected belongs to TAJ, not to the firm.

questions.q: Kirk worries that the bank could take his house if the company cannot pay its debts. What is the position?
o: As a director he must pay all the company's debts himself
Either owner's house can be taken, as in any partnership
The debts are the company's, unless he signed a guarantee
A company cannot borrow money, so the problem cannot arise
questions.why: A limited company is a separate legal person, so its owners' liability is limited to what they put in. But lenders often ask directors to sign a personal guarantee, and a director who signs one can be made to pay that debt from his own assets.

questions.q: What do Omari's records most clearly support?
o: Taking on his first employee, as work and cash are steady
Raising all his prices by 30% to cut down the enquiries
Dropping maintenance contracts to focus on installations
Taking every enquiry himself by working even longer hours
questions.why: Sales above plan, jobs turned away and a balance that never fell below two months of costs show steady work and the cash to pay a wage. Maintenance contracts are his most profitable work for the hours, so he should keep and grow them.

questions.q: What does the reversed polarity found at testing suggest Omari should change first?
o: Skip testing on small jobs, so he has more time to rest
Buy a new tester, since the old one must have misled him
Ask each client to check the polarity at the end of every job
Cut his hours and share the work, as fatigue causes errors
questions.why: His testing worked: it caught the error. The cause was most likely tiredness from 70-hour weeks, and the next tired mistake might not be caught. Reducing his hours and sharing the work protects clients, the firm and himself; testing must never be cut.

questions.q: What does Omari's success rate with quotations most likely suggest?
o: His marketing is weak, since too few clients contact him
His prices may be too low, leaving profit on the table
His prices are too high and should be cut even further
He should stop sending written quotations altogether
questions.why: Winning almost every quotation usually means the price is lower than clients would happily pay, and he turns away work, so demand is strong. He should compare actual profit on finished jobs with his estimates and check competitors' prices; a modest rise may lose a few jobs but raise profit and ease his hours.

questions.q: Courtney trades as a sole trader. His business owes a supplier J$900,000 that it cannot pay. What is the position?
o: Only the business's tools and van can be taken, not his home
The debt falls away, because the business name is registered
He is personally liable: his savings and home are at risk
The supplier must wait until the business makes a profit
questions.why: A sole trader and the business are the same legal person, so the owner has unlimited liability for its debts. Registering a business name does not change this; it is one reason some owners form a limited company as the firm and its debts grow.

questions.q: A contractor's gross profit rose this year, but her net profit fell. What is the most likely cause?
o: Her overheads rose by more than her gross profit did
Material prices on her jobs rose faster than her prices
She finished fewer jobs this year than she did last year
Several clients paid their invoices later than usual
questions.why: Gross profit is sales less the direct costs of the jobs; net profit is gross profit less overheads. Since gross profit rose, the jobs did better, so the fall must come from overheads. Dearer materials or fewer jobs would lower gross profit, and late payment affects cash, not profit.
